newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: U.S. ambassador reassures Nicaragua on deportations.
newsitem.headline: U.S. ambassador reassures Nicaragua on deportations.

text.p: The U.S. ambassador to Nicaragua said on Thursday that Washington did not plan a mass deportation of Nicaraguan political exiles now that a pro-U.S. government has been elected in Managua.

U.S. Ambassador Lino Gutierrez's statement came amid local press reports the United States planned a mass deportation of Nicaraguan exiles after a family of four was sent back to Nicaragua on Wednesday.
"President (Bill) Clinton has clearly said there will be no mass deportations from the United States," Gutierrez said.

Gutierrez said Washington would apply its immigration laws in a normal fashion. Moreover, lengthy appeals that can take months or years, made it unreasonable to expect a flood of Nicaraguans would be sent home in the near future.

In the late 1970s and 1980s, when the left-wing Sandinista government ruled Nicaragua, thousands of Nicaraguans sought political asylum in the United States. There are an estimated 200,000 Nicaraguans living in the Miami region alone.
Now, with back-to-back democratic elections in Nicaragua and the inauguration of a pro-U.S. government, many of these Nicaraguans fear deportation.
"It is the same policy that we have applied in recent years; there has been no change with the victory of Aleman," Gutierrez said.

In his inaugural address on Jan. 10, Aleman called on foreign governments to let Nicaraguan exiles stay where they were since Nicaragua's impoverished economy and infrastructure could not support a mass return of exiles.

"For these brothers we make a very personal, special and official call on the friendly governments of the countries in which they live, to offer them with benevolence their generous understanding and human solidarity," Aleman said.

A spokeswoman for Nicaragua's Foreign Ministry, Claudia Paniagua, told Reuters that in 1996 only 177 illegal Nicaraguan immigrants were deported from the United States and 151 were rejected on arrival at the United States border.
So far in 1997, four Nicaraguans have been deported, she said.
